entry.title: CFTC staff advisory warns designated contract markets against broad, template-style self-certifications of event contract series

category.term: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (Division of Market Oversight)

entry.content:
On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission's Division of Market Oversight (DMO) issued an advisory reminding designated contract markets (DCMs) about the proper procedures for submitting self-certifications of an event contract series. The advisory addresses concerns about the practice of submitting broad, template-style certifications that combine many potential event contract variations into a single certification. According to the advisory, this approach limits DMO's ability to determine whether a DCM has provided all the information, explanation, and analysis required by Commission Regulation Section 40.2, and whether it has adequately evaluated the settlement methodology, data sources, and core-principles compliance of any contract it intends to list. The guidance reiterates that broad, template-style certifications should not be submitted, and explains when closely related event contracts may be certified as a class or submitted for approval under Commission Regulations Sections 40.2(d) or 40.3. The advisory was issued as CFTC Staff Letter No. 26-22.
Primary source: CFTC Press Release 9273-26 (Division of Market Oversight advisory; CFTC Staff Letter No. 26-22) — July 24, 2026 — https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/9273-26
Relevant to: prediction-market operators and other designated contract markets that list event contracts, and their compliance/listing teams — self-certification submissions must provide full per-contract Reg 40.2 analysis rather than broad template-style filings

entry.title: OCC denies Wise's application for a US national trust bank charter, citing AML/CFT compliance deficiencies and a July 2025 multi-state consent order; Wise shares fall ~10%

category.term: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)

entry.content:
On July 24, 2026, Wise plc announced via London Stock Exchange regulatory news service (RNS) that the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) communicated its decision to deny Wise's application for a national trust bank charter. The OCC cited significant supervisory and compliance concerns, including management's demonstrated persistent inability to manage anti-money laundering and terrorism financing risks, directors and management lacking sufficient AML/CFT experience, proposed activities presenting high AML/CFT risks, and organizers failing to demonstrate sufficient experience with banking regulations related to fiduciary activities. The OCC letter references historical issues with the original application and a multi-state consent order Wise entered into in July 2025. Wise shares fell approximately 10-11% on Nasdaq following the announcement. Wise stated it plans to submit a new application under a GENIUS Act framework. Wise's existing money transmission licenses (MTLs) across 48 US states and 4 territories are unaffected; the denial pertains solely to the proposed national trust charter. The Bank Policy Institute and banking trade groups had submitted opposition letters. The OCC's denial letter has not been separately published by the OCC on occ.gov as of this date.

entry.title: OFAC designates 4 individuals and 9 entities supporting Iranian digital asset exchanges Zedcex and Zedxion; Istanbul fintech Zedpay and Dubai-based Zedx DMCC among designees

category.term: U.S. Department of the Treasury / OFAC

entry.content:
On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated four individuals and nine entities that form key components of Babak Zanjani's Iranian sanctions evasion network. The action targets support infrastructure for the previously-designated digital asset exchanges Zedcex Exchange Limited and Zedxion Exchange Limited (both designated January 30, 2026). OFAC stated that multiple Zedcex and Zedxion-attributed addresses have processed funds on behalf of wallets attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Among the newly designated entities is Istanbul-based Zedpay Finansal Sistem Ve Hizmetleri Anonim Sirketi (Zedpay), a financial technology company that provided digital wallet and global transfer services and was directly integrated into the Zedxion trading platform, giving Zedxion fiat settlement and cross-border payment capabilities. Dubai-based Zedx DMCC acted on Zedcex's behalf with regard to Zedcex's exchange wallets. Dubai-based BZ Diamond FZCO, a diamond dealer managed by Zanjani's sister Bahareh Morteza Zanjani, conducted transactions with Zedxion and Zedcex wallets and promoted Zedxion's NFT marketplace. Six Iran-based entities comprising the Dot One conglomerate are also designated, including DotOne Gold Company, which operates Tala Token (an allegedly gold-backed digital asset token); significant quantities of Tala Token passed through Zedcex infrastructure in early 2025. Designated individuals: Mehdi Rezazadeh (Zedpay chairperson, Istanbul), Sukhrob Oimakhmadov (Zedx DMCC manager, Dubai), Bahareh Morteza Zanjani (BZ Diamond FZCO manager, Dubai), and Solmaz Bani (registered websites for Zanjani companies). Designations issued pursuant to Executive Order 13902.
Primary source: U.S. Department of the Treasury Press Release sb0576 — July 24, 2026 — https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0576

entry.title: OFAC designates Hamas money exchange El-Kahira for General Trading (Turkiye) that serviced 'both fiat and cryptocurrencies'; 7 total designees in Hamas/Muslim Brotherhood action

category.term: U.S. Department of the Treasury / OFAC

entry.content:
On July 23, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated a senior Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood (EMB) official, along with three individuals and three entities that provided material support to Hamas. Among the designated entities is Turkiye-based El-Kahira for General Trading, which OFAC states provided underground banking services, 'servicing both fiat and cryptocurrencies,' to Hamas and to known Sweden-based organized crime groups including the Foxtrot Network. El-Kahira transferred hundreds of thousands of dollars for Hamas. El-Kahira's owner Khuldun Khamis Zakaria Alden and shareholders Zaid Issam Ahmed Al-Jebouri and Abdullah Issam Ahmad Al-Jebouri are also designated. The two other designated entities are Tujah Bulah Global (Indonesia, also known as Seven Spikes Global, a Hamas fundraising charity) and Madad Palestine Charitable Society (Gaza, a Hamas front charity whose funds were diverted to Hamas's military wing). The designated EMB official is Mahmoud al-Abyari, UK-based Secretary General of the Muslim Brotherhood General Secretariat. Designations issued pursuant to Executive Order 13224, as amended. This action follows prior Hamas/MB OFAC actions on January 21, 2026 and March 12, 2026.

entry.title: SEC agrees to pay $150,000 and produce records to settle Coinbase FOIA lawsuit; settlement confirms Gensler texts deleted 2022-2023 and 21 officials' phones wiped

category.term: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission

entry.content:
The SEC and History Associates Inc. (acting on behalf of Coinbase) filed a joint status report on July 22, 2026 in History Associates Inc. v. SEC (D.D.C. No. 1:24-cv-01766), settling a FOIA lawsuit over SEC records on Ethereum and Gensler-era communications. Settlement terms: SEC pays $150,000 in legal fees; SEC produces all remaining responsive documents; case dismissed upon completion. The lawsuit (filed June 2024) compelled production of thousands of SEC records. The production confirmed that SEC Chair Gensler's text messages were deleted for October 2022 through September 2023 and that 21 senior SEC officials' phones were wiped. Two previously withheld documents were released in settlement. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong called it 'a huge win for crypto.' Reported by CoinDesk, CoinTelegraph, CryptoSlate, and FinanceFeeds (all July 23, 2026); underlying joint status report filed in PACER.

entry.title: Reported: New would-be-final CLARITY Act draft circulated July 22 with DOJ-enforced ethics ban on federal officials issuing digital assets

category.term: U.S. Senate (as reported)

entry.content:
As reported by CoinDesk on July 22, 2026 and corroborated by CNBC, Roll Call, American Banker and Disruption Banking the same day, lawmakers circulated a would-be-final draft of the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act as the U.S. Senate prepared for floor action before its August recess. The draft includes a conflict-of-interest section barring the President, Vice President, members of Congress, federal judges and their spouses from issuing or sponsoring digital assets for pay while in office; per CNBC, the Department of Justice would enforce the ban with fines of up to $250,000 per day and disgorgement of profits plus a penalty of up to 10% of amounts received. The ethics provision is set to sunset January 20, 2029 and would require regulators to implement it within one year of enactment. Per CoinDesk, the draft retains the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (non-custodial developers not treated as money transmitters) and adds new language on federal preemption, provisional registration and commodity pool operators. Senate Majority Leader John Thune's office said he intends to move to floor action in the coming days; the draft text was posted at Punchbowl News but had not been shared with Democratic lawmakers, several of whom criticized the DOJ-enforced ethics mechanism. The bill needs 60 Senate votes.

entry.title: SEC Commissioner Peirce: some crypto vaults and onchain lending strategies may fall within federal securities laws

category.term: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (Commissioner Hester M. Peirce)

entry.content:
On July 22, 2026, SEC Commissioner Hester M. Peirce issued a statement titled 'Headstands and Summervaults: A Statement on Crypto Vaults and Lending Strategies,' stating that crypto vaults and onchain lending strategies may fall within the federal securities laws depending on how they are structured and managed. Peirce wrote that moving activities within the scope of the securities laws onchain 'as a general matter, does not take those activities outside the scope,' and that 'tokenized securities are still securities. That principle holds for vaults.' She said parties who manage vaults (for example, by selecting yield-generating activities, re-allocating assets, or selecting the parties that make those decisions) or lending strategies (for example, by setting interest rates, deciding which assets to accommodate, and setting loan-to-value limits and liquidation thresholds) may want to analyze whether their activities implicate the securities laws; that a vault could be a common enterprise or fall into investment company territory and involvement may implicate investment adviser requirements; and that onchain loans could bear the hallmarks of notes that are securities. She stated the analysis turns on the specific facts and circumstances and invited market participants to engage with the SEC. The statement is an individual Commissioner statement, not a Commission rule or enforcement action.

entry.title: House Agriculture subcommittee examines prediction market customer protections and CFTC authority over sports event contracts

category.term: U.S. House Committee on Agriculture, Subcommittee on Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development

entry.content:
The Subcommittee on Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development held a hearing titled 'Examining Prediction Markets: Customer Protections and Market Integrity in Sports Event Markets' on July 21, 2026, chaired by Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-SD). Five witnesses testified: Robert Schwartz (partner, Morgan Lewis; former CFTC general counsel), Carl Kennedy (derivatives attorney, Katten Muchin Rosenman), Chris Cylke (SVP government relations, American Gaming Association), David Bean (chairman, Indian Gaming Association), and Asaf Meir (co-founder and CEO, Solidus Labs). Schwartz and Kennedy defended CFTC jurisdiction under the Commodity Exchange Act; Cylke and Bean argued sports event contracts are gambling subject to state police powers and the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, with Bean urging advancement of H.R. 7840 (Event Contract Enforcement Act). Cylke cited Kalshi's sports-related trading volume exceeding $111 billion through H1 2026 and noted that 45% of all online sports betting advertising now comes from prediction market operators. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-MI) pressed witnesses on the CFTC's order directing Kalshi to defy a Michigan state court order; Schwartz described the order as extraordinary, stating: 'It certainly was a flex.' Rep. Angie Craig (D-MN) questioned whether a single-commissioner CFTC had the capability to police prediction markets given proposed budget cuts. Chairman Johnson closed by stating: 'Courts are acting in this space. The commission is acting in this space. I do not think that this committee, Congress, should be silent. We have an obligation to drive toward finding out what is the common ground.' Testimony documents are posted at agriculture.house.gov.

entry.title: Washington State Court Grants Preliminary Injunction Against Kalshi for Violations of State Gambling Act and Consumer Protection Act

category.term: Washington State Office of the Attorney General / King County Superior Court

entry.content:
King County Superior Court (Washington state) granted a preliminary injunction against Kalshi on July 20, 2026, finding that Kalshi's prediction market contracts likely violate both the Washington Gambling Act and the Consumer Protection Act. The court found that Kalshi's event contracts — covering sports, elections, natural disasters, and other contingent events — constitute gambling under Washington law, which defines gambling as staking or risking something of value upon the outcome of a contest of chance or a future contingent event, and prohibits internet gambling as amended in 2006. The court also ruled that Kalshi's marketing constitutes unfair and deceptive acts or practices under the Consumer Protection Act, citing a Kalshi advertisement in which a user texts about finding 'a way to bet on the NFL even though we live in Washington.' Washington AG Nick Brown filed the underlying complaint on March 27, 2026. The court will issue a final injunction order setting full remedies on August 5, 2026. Washington is reported as the 4th state to obtain a preliminary injunction against Kalshi's sports event contracts, with state regulators and courts prevailing in 19 of 23 such decisions nationally.

entry.title: FTC: Celsius Network founders to pay $16.5 million; banned from marketing asset deposit and withdrawal products

category.term: Federal Trade Commission

entry.content:
The FTC announced on July 20, 2026 that Alexander Mashinsky, former CEO of cryptocurrency platform Celsius Network Inc., and business partners Shlomi Daniel Leon and Hanoch "Nuke" Goldstein will pay a total of $16.5 million to resolve FTC charges that they deceived users by falsely promising that deposits made to their cryptocurrency platform would be safe and always available. Mashinsky pays $10 million, Leon $4.1 million and Goldstein $2.4 million. Mashinsky and Leon also agreed to a ban on marketing or selling products or services that can be used to deposit, exchange, invest or withdraw assets; Goldstein agreed to a ban covering retail products or services used to buy, sell, deposit, withdraw, distribute or trade cryptocurrency. The orders, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, also prohibit misrepresentations about any product or service and violations of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. The Commission vote on the Mashinsky order was 3-0; the votes on the Leon and Goldstein orders were 2-0.

entry.title: FDIC publishes GENIUS Act PPSI reporting forms for PRA comment (FR Doc. 2026-14589, 91 FR 45274)

category.term: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

entry.content:
On July 20, 2026 (filed on public inspection July 17), the FDIC published a Paperwork Reduction Act notice (FR Doc. 2026-14589, 91 FR 45274) requesting 60-day public comment on proposed weekly and quarterly reporting forms for FDIC-supervised Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers (PPSIs). The notice is associated with the FDIC's GENIUS Act PPSI NPRM (April 10, 2026, 91 FR 18534). Weekly Form PS-01 (for PPSIs with $1 billion or more in total outstanding issuance value or $100 million or more in average daily transaction volume) includes eight schedules covering top holders, top exchanges, trading volume, top counterparties, capital, issuance and redemption, and reserve assets disaggregated by type (cash and deposits, U.S. Treasuries by CUSIP, reverse repurchase agreements, money market mutual funds, and other instruments). Weekly Form PS-01a (smaller PPSIs) has three schedules. Quarterly Form PS-02 covers income statement, balance sheet, off-balance sheet items, capital and operational backstop, and memoranda including blockchain activity, redemption metrics, and custody activities. The FDIC estimates approximately 30 FDIC-supervised institutions would perform PPSI activities; ongoing weekly reporting burden estimated at 2,080 hours per year and quarterly at 800 hours. The publication confirms the FDIC GENIUS Act implementing final rule was not published as of the July 18, 2026 statutory one-year deadline. Comment period closes September 18, 2026.

entry.title: Fed Chair Warsh testifies to House Financial Services: no Federal Reserve bailout for crypto or stablecoins; Fed 'racing' to meet GENIUS Act stablecoin rulemaking deadline; nonbank fintech payment access pressed

category.term: Federal Reserve Board

entry.content:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh testified before the House Committee on Financial Services on July 14, 2026, as part of the Semiannual Monetary Policy Report (2128 Rayburn House Office Building, 10:00 AM). The official prepared statement focused on price stability, monetary policy, and internal Fed task forces. During the Q&A, Warsh made three statements directly relevant to crypto, stablecoin, and fintech operators: (1) No Federal Reserve bailout for crypto or stablecoins: Pressed by Rep. Brad Sherman on whether the Fed would provide the kind of support it gave money market funds in 2008, Warsh stated 'We do not want to be in the bailout business, full stop.' He added that the Fed would 'do everything we can to mitigate... extraordinary risks' but would not bail out crypto. He did not fully rule out marginal systemic-spillover mitigation. (2) GENIUS Act rulemaking urgency: Warsh told lawmakers the Fed is 'racing' to finalize its portion of the GENIUS Act stablecoin implementing rules ahead of the July 18, 2026 one-year statutory deadline. The deadline has since been confirmed missed (the Federal Register contains no in-scope publication; July 18 is a Saturday; earliest possible publication is Monday July 20). (3) Nonbank fintech payment-system access: Rep. Sherman separately pressed on Kraken's pending bank application and nonbank crypto firms seeking direct access to the payment system; Warsh invoked systemic-risk considerations without making a specific commitment. Background: Warsh is the most crypto-sympathetic Fed Chair on record, having previously disclosed venture stakes in Bitcoin payments, a crypto index manager, Bitwise, and a stablecoin venture â all divested under Fed ethics rules prior to confirmation in May 2026. A 2026 New York Fed staff report cited in contemporaneous coverage found stablecoin activity can transmit liquidity stress to banks and complicate monetary policy. This is Warsh's first congressional testimony since his confirmation. entry.title: SCOTUS rules 6-3 that for-cause removal protections for SEC and CFTC commissioners are unconstitutional (Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332)

category.term: U.S. Supreme Court

entry.content:
On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court of the United States issued its 6-3 opinion in Trump v. Slaughter (No. 25-332), authored by Chief Justice Roberts, overturning Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935). The Court held that the for-cause removal protection in the FTC's enabling statute — and by structural extension the SEC and CFTC, which operate under identical removal provisions — is contrary to the separation of powers under the Constitution. Effective immediately, the President may remove SEC and CFTC commissioners without cause. A companion order in Trump v. Cook (No. 25A312, June 29, 2026) denied a government application to stay a preliminary injunction protecting Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook; the Federal Reserve's statutory structure was not directly addressed by the majority opinion. The opinion is published on the Court's official slip opinion list for October Term 2025.
